SEASON_LINE handle week 1's big picture; these stay street-level.

weeks.0,1: Somebody has chalked hopscotch squares on the cannery dock, tide-washed to ghosts. School starts Monday and everyone is pretending it doesn't.
weeks.0,2: The Silva boat came in heavy twice this week. Men you haven't met nod at you on the boardwalk like you've always been here.
weeks.0,3: First real rain. The gutters on Alder Street sing all night and the teacher keeps the stove going by ten a.m.
weeks.0,4: A seal has taken up residence under the fuel dock. The harbormaster says shoot it; nobody shoots it; everyone brings it fish heads.
weeks.1,1: The fall run fills the river like a rumor coming true. You can hear the cannery line from the schoolyard, a sound like rain on tin that never lets up.
weeks.1,2: Overtime week. Half your class is asleep at their desks because their fathers are on the boats and their mothers are on the line.
weeks.1,3: The first southerly of the season takes a skiff off its mooring and lays it politely on the beach, upside down, like a joke.
weeks.1,4: Halloween. The town does it properly — the cannery office gives out saltwater taffy and Mr. Aandahl wears the same rubber mask he has worn since the war, whichever war that was.
weeks.2,1: Frost on the boardwalk in the mornings now. The puddles hold a skin of ice until the school bell and give it up by noon.
weeks.2,2: The last big tide of the run. Boats you've never seen before crowd the harbor, and the cafe runs out of pie by eleven.
weeks.2,3: The line stopped on Friday afternoon and nobody went back to work. Flags at half-staff on the school, the cannery, the Grange. Vovo lights a candle and doesn't explain it to you, which is how you know.
weeks.2,4: Thanksgiving. The town smells of woodsmoke and crab. Whoever has no family gets collected by somebody who does; that is simply how it works here.
weeks.3,1: The rain arrives like a job it intends to keep. Third day of it the school roof starts a slow drip into a bucket by the coat rack, plink, all day.
weeks.3,2: The men are home now, boats hauled out, and the town feels crowded and warm and slightly too loud, like a kitchen before a holiday.
weeks.3,3: Christmas trees come down from the hills on the log truck, roped like a catch. The Grange hall smells of fir and coffee for two weeks straight.
weeks.3,4: Christmas week. Lights in the windows along the harbor so the whole town doubles itself in the black water. Midnight mass is standing room.
weeks.4,1: New year. The minus tides come at dawn and the flats crawl with lanterns — the whole town out in boots, breath showing, digging by feel.
weeks.4,2: A whale went by on Tuesday, close in. School let out to watch. The teacher called it geography and nobody argued.
weeks.4,3: Chimney-fire weather. The volunteer brigade gets two calls in one week and Mr. Lindqvist's roof will need shakes come spring.
weeks.4,4: The cold clamps down. The puddle ice holds all day now and the kids skate the flooded field behind the Grange on cardboard and dares.
weeks.5,1: The storms line up offshore like ships waiting for a berth. Between them the light is thin and clean and the beach is re-drawn every morning.
weeks.5,2: A freighter lost deck cargo somewhere north and the beach pays out lumber for a week. Half the town's fences will be built of it by summer.
weeks.5,3: The big one hits on a Thursday night. The power goes and stays gone two days; the town runs on lamps and gossip and does not much mind.
weeks.5,4: After the storm, the beach is a museum of elsewhere: glass floats, a doll's head, a door. Del says the sea returns everything eventually, just never to the right people.
weeks.6,1: The river runs brown and fat with the hills' rain. Men stand on the bridge watching it the way they watch a fire — quiet, hands in pockets.
weeks.6,2: High water. The road to the valley closes at the slough and the school bus becomes a boat schedule. Nobody panics; everybody talks about it.
weeks.6,3: Sandbags at the cannery's lower doors. The old-timers name past floods like relatives — the '48, the '55 — and rank this one politely below them.
weeks.6,4: The water stands down. What it leaves is mud and one stranded piano, upright on the flats, that nobody ever claims and everybody photographs.
weeks.7,1: The alders go green in one week, all together, like they voted. The hills look suddenly younger.
weeks.7,2: Herring in the bay. The water goes silver-black with them at dusk and the gulls lose their minds entirely.
weeks.7,3: The boats go back in the water one by one, fresh-painted, riding high. The harbor smells of copper paint and hope.
weeks.7,4: Easter. New shoes, wet lawns, egg dye in every kitchen sink. Vovo's sweet bread makes the whole street smell like a bakery in another country.
weeks.8,1: The salmonberry blooms pink along every creek draw, first color of the year. The town is named for it and acts like it forgot, but everyone slows down on the bridge.
weeks.8,2: The first berries, red-gold and watery-sweet. Kids come to school with stained fingers, and the teacher has given up on that battle.
weeks.8,3: Shearwater weather — long bright evenings, the sea flat as poured metal. Supper happens late all over town because nobody will come indoors.
weeks.8,4: The seniors paint the water tower. It is tradition, it is illegal, and the sheriff parks where he can't quite see it happen.
weeks.9,1: School lets out and the town fills with bicycles. The travelling show's trucks roll in at dawn and by supper there is a Ferris wheel over the cannery lot, improbable as a giraffe.
weeks.9,2: The show runs every evening. Music carries clear across the water so the whole harbor has a soundtrack, tinny and brave.
weeks.9,3: The days are so long the light seems to be showing off. You know every dog in this town by name now, and they know you.
weeks.9,4: Last week. The show is striking its tents, and the fortune-teller's sign is already down. The town looks the way it did in September, except that now it looks like yours.
